patient_counselling: PRELOAD NSAIDs for best effect: start 24–48 hours BEFORE expected period onset (or at the very first sign of pain/spotting), continue scheduled (not PRN) for the first 2–3 days of bleeding — preloading inhibits prostaglandin synthesis before peak release.

Naproxen 500 mg loading dose, then 250 mg every 6–8 hours (max 1250 mg/day) — longer half-life, fewer doses; OR ibuprofen 400–600 mg every 6 hours (max 2400 mg/day); OR mefenamic acid 500 mg loading then 250 mg every 6 hours (dual mechanism — COX inhibition + prostaglandin receptor antagonism — particularly effective).
Take NSAIDs WITH FOOD or milk to reduce stomach upset; do NOT exceed maximum daily dose; do not combine multiple NSAIDs.

NSAID cautions: avoid in active peptic ulcer disease, severe renal/hepatic impairment, history of NSAID-induced asthma, last trimester of pregnancy, anticoagulant use without medical guidance; use lowest effective dose; consider PPI co-therapy if high GI risk.
Topical heat (heating pad or hot water bottle on lower abdomen, 15–20 minutes at a time) is comparable to ibuprofen for mild dysmenorrhea — combine with NSAIDs for additive benefit.
Regular aerobic exercise (brisk walking, yoga, swimming 30 min, 3–5×/week) reduces dysmenorrhea over time per Cochrane review; reduce dietary salt and caffeine before/during periods.

If NSAIDs alone are insufficient or contraindicated: hormonal options (combined oral contraceptive pill — continuous or skip-placebo regimen; levonorgestrel IUS — Mirena/Kyleena) are second-line and require physician/NP prescription. Excellent long-term option for chronic dysmenorrhea.
Adjuncts with modest evidence: omega-3 (1000 mg/day), vitamin B1 (100 mg/day), magnesium (250 mg/day), TENS unit (high-frequency for pain relief). Discuss with pharmacist before starting.

Red flags — see physician: severe pain not responding to NSAIDs after 2–3 cycles, new-onset or worsening pain pattern (especially if previously stable — suggests secondary dysmenorrhea: endometriosis, fibroids, adenomyosis), pain outside of menstruation or during intercourse, heavy bleeding with clots, fever + pelvic pain (PID), suspected pregnancy.
Track your cycles and pain pattern (paper diary or app) — useful for ongoing management and for physician referral if needed.
therapeutic_flow: 1. Confirm Minor Ailments eligibility: Ontario resident, typical primary dysmenorrhea presentation (cyclic pelvic pain coinciding with menstruation, onset usually within 1–2 years of menarche); verify ID/OHIP, obtain consent.

2. Focused history: pain characterization (timing, severity, duration, quality), age at menarche, cycle regularity, bleeding pattern (heavy, clots), associated symptoms (nausea, headache, diarrhea), prior treatments and response, current medications, contraceptive needs/use, pregnancy possibility.

3. Red flag screen: pain outside menstruation, dyspareunia (endometriosis), heavy menstrual bleeding with clots, fever + pelvic pain (PID), new-onset or worsening pain pattern after previously stable cycles (secondary dysmenorrhea), suspected pregnancy, NSAID contraindications — refer.
4. Differential diagnosis: rule out endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids, ovarian cysts, pelvic inflammatory disease, ectopic pregnancy, IBS, interstitial cystitis, copper IUD-related pain.

5. Therapy selection: NSAID preloading (naproxen, ibuprofen, or mefenamic acid) starting 24–48h before menses + scheduled dosing × 2–3 days; topical heat as adjunct; lifestyle measures; refer for hormonal options if NSAIDs contraindicated or insufficient.
6. Counsel on preloading concept, NSAID technique (with food, max dose, contraindications), heat therapy, exercise, cycle tracking, expected onset of relief, when to escalate.
7. Document the encounter per OCP standards: assessment findings, diagnosis (primary dysmenorrhea), therapy chosen, counselling provided, notify primary care provider.

8. Follow-up: reassess after 2–3 cycles; if inadequate response, refer for hormonal therapy (COC, LNG-IUS) consideration; if features of secondary dysmenorrhea emerge, refer to gynecology for workup (TVUS, lap).
